chunks: Why chips can't be arbitrarily large. The question: Why can't ginormous chips, single die be made? What are some challenges and workarounds?
A chip cannot be made arbitrarily large for two main reasons.
First, the machine that prints chip patterns exposes only a fixed area at a time, about 26 mm by 33 mm, which is about 858 mm².
Second, bigger dies are more likely to be ruined by a defect, so the cost of each working chip climbs steeply. The usual fix is several smaller dies in one package.
A rubber stamp has a fixed size, so it cannot print a bigger picture in one press. That is the hard limit. Now suppose any speck of dust on a printed picture ruins it.
A huge picture is almost sure to catch a speck, while a small one often escapes. That is the cost limit.
Above the reticle limit the options are special stitching or partitioning.
Partitioning produces multi-die modules whose dies are tested before assembly so that one bad die doesn't waste the rest.
Reticle: the pattern plate that the printing machine projects onto the wafer. It sets the biggest single die. Yield: the fraction of dies that work.
Defect density: serious flaws per square centimeter of wafer. Chiplet: a small die built to be joined with others in one package.
Known good die: a die tested before assembly, so bad ones are never packaged.
Use illustrative numbers: a USD 10,000 wafer and 0. 1 defects per cm². A 100 mm² die yields about 90%, and about 640 fit on a 300 mm wafer, so each good die costs about USD 17.
A full-size 858 mm² die yields only about 42%, and only about 59 fit, so each good die costs about USD 400. That is 8. 6 times the area but about 23 times the cost.
Now build the same design as four chiplets, each about 236 mm² (a quarter of the area plus 10% for the links between them).
Each yields about 79%, and the four cost about USD 200 in silicon. That is roughly half, and each chiplet is tested first. That is the whole idea.
"The hard limit is the reticle: the scanner exposes about 26 by 33 millimetres, around 858 square millimetres, in one shot.
The softer, economic limit is yield: it falls exponentially with area, so an 858 square millimetre die yields about 42% at 0.
1 defects per cm² versus 90% at 100 square millimetres, and fewer dies fit on a wafer, so cost per good die is about 20 times higher.
Workarounds: chiplets in one package with short, wide die-to-die links, tested before assembly; redundancy; and for wafer-scale chips, tiny repeated cores with spares and routing around defects."
